title: Pleasure without the hook
hookLine: the monk is taught to eat like a traveler eating to cross the desert

cards: A fair warning first: today's image is meant to be hard to hear. The early texts sometimes reach for a shocking picture on purpose, so a point can't slide past. Eleven days ago, giving food was life itself.
Today, the other side: eating, and the hook that can hide in it. The bag of chips that empties itself. The second dessert nobody wanted.

In the Connected Sayings, in a chapter on what the texts call the four kinds of nutriment, the Buddha asks the monks how they should regard their daily food, and answers with a parable about two travelers in a desert.

teach.h: FOOD RUNS OUT IN THE DESERT.
teach.b: A husband and wife set out across a desert with a little food, and with their only son, a child they love dearly. Halfway across, the food runs out, and there is no other way to survive.

In the parable, they do the unthinkable: weeping, they eat their own child's flesh, to reach the other side. Would they eat that food for fun, the Buddha asks, for pleasure, for decoration, for beauty?
No, the monks answer: only to cross the desert. That, he says, is how to regard ordinary food. The image is deliberately unbearable.
Nobody could enjoy that meal, and nobody would take one bite more than needed. That's the point.

teach.h: NOT FOR FUN, NOT FOR LOOKS.
teach.b: Monks still say a daily reflection, found elsewhere in the canon, that carries the same sense in gentler words: I eat not for fun, not for intoxication, not for looks, but only to keep this body going, to end hunger, and to support the holy life.
The teaching isn't that food is bad, or that taste is wrong; lay Buddhists cook beautiful food and offer it with joy.
The hook is the extra: eating to fill a mood, to escape, to keep chasing a pleasure that ended three bites ago. So the parable asks a simple question at every meal: what is this for?
If the answer is to cross, to live, to be well, the pleasure that comes with it has no hook in it.

how: Theravada monks and nuns recite a daily reflection on the purpose of food before eating, and many lay Buddhists practice mindful eating, pausing before a meal to consider what it is for.

o: nutriment, the food that keeps us going
a fast kept to purify the body
a feast offered to honor the gods

games.q: pleasure without the hook: tap the pairs.
p: not for fun, not for looks

s: the parable teaches that taste and food are evil
it's about why we eat: just enough to cross, not to chase pleasure.
monks recite a reflection on the purpose of food
not for fun or looks, but to sustain the body and the holy life.
the desert parable sits in a chapter on four kinds of nutriment
edible food is the first of the four.

games.q: the desert travelers have no choice but to eat this terrible food. how do they eat it?
o: only enough to cross the desert.
all at once, to be done with it.
games.why: not for fun, not for beauty, only to reach the other side. the Buddha says to regard ordinary food the same way.

practice: Picture your next meal on the table in front of you, and before you eat, ask the parable's question: what is this for? Let the honest answer come, hunger, energy, comfort, company.
Then picture eating slowly, tasting each bite, and noticing the moment you've had enough: not when the plate is empty, but when you've crossed.

wordCard.voice: ahara. The Pali and Sanskrit word for nutriment or food, behind the parable of the desert travelers in the Connected Sayings: eat as they did, only to cross, and the meal has no hook in it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali ahara: nutriment, food, literally 'what is brought in'; the four nutriments sustain beings.

carryVoice: Your line: just enough to cross. Food isn't the hook; the extra is. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 2 (Sabbasava Sutta), reflection on food
